newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 17.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- INFLATION HELD DOWN TO 2.5 PER CENT

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has resisted pressure to raise interest rates, claiming that the strength of sterling is itself sufficiently anti-inflationary. Speaking after his regular briefing with the governor of the Bank of England, Clarke said: 'I decided to make no change'. The decision has fuelled speculation that interest rates may not now be changed until after the general election.
-- HORLICK SAYS PROMOTED BEFORE SHE WAS SUSPENDED

Nicola Horlick, the top fund manager who was suspended by Morgan Grenfell Asset Management on Tuesday, has resigned as a director of the group. In an interview with the Financial Times, Horlick claimed she had been promoted just days before the dismissal following demands from fund managers that she be given more authority.
-- FORD TO SHED 1,300 JOBS AT ITS HALEWOOD PLANT

Ford has appealed for 1,300 voluntary redundancies at its Halewood plant on Merseyside, after announcing that the factory will not produce the next-generation Escort model. Ford, the leading car company in the UK, is looking to stem European losses and blamed the measure on a need to cut costs because of the decline in its UK market share and the severe overcapacity in the European motor industry.
-- BUSINESS PRESSES FOR NEW ROYAL YACHT

Business leaders, MPs and peers are putting the government under formidable pressure to replace the royal yacht Brittania, which is due to be decommissioned later this year. The lobbyists point to the role the yacht has played in promoting UK trade worldwide, with some estimates claiming it has helped raise about 2 billion stg for British business in the last 10 years. Ministers are understood to have no real plans for a replacement, with claims putting the cost of building a new yacht at about 80 million stg.
-- SHELL TO INVEST IN GLOBAL POWER GENERATION MARKET

Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell has revealed substantial investment plans in the emerging $700 billion global power generation market. The group, which has a cash pile of $8.35 billion to draw on, is looking to exploit its natural gas and coal assets over the next five years, initially in markets such as the Philippines and Namibia. However, the group could also look towards mature markets, and a move into power generation in the UK is expected by industry observers.
-- BRUSSELS TAX PROPOSAL ALARMS TELECOMS GROUPS

A delegation of representatives from European telecoms companies, including AT&T, BT and the Global One alliance, is to meet with European Commission officials in Brussels to express their concern over a tax proposal. The Commission is planning to close a tax loophole which will leave telecoms suppliers registered for VAT in the EU at a commercial disadvantage to their non-EU competitors who choose not to register.
-- FOWLER CONDEMNS PLANS FOR 1 BILLION STERLING PLANT

Plans for a 1 billion stg semiconductor plant to be built near Birmingham, in the centre of the UK, have been blasted by Sir Norman Fowler, a former chairman of the Conservative party. Sir Norman was speaking at a public inquiry into the proposed 137-acre development, which would be built on a greenfield site in his local constituency. Dutch electronics giant Philips is thought to be one of several electronics companies understood to be examining the site. Sir Norman claimed that Labour-controlled Birmingham council is backing the development for political and financial gain.
-- WERNER QUITS AS MERCEDES CHIEF

Helmut Werner has resigned as chief executive of German automotive giant Mercedes-Benz, after losing a power struggle with Jurgen Schrempp, chairman of Mercedes' parent company Daimler-Benz. Werner is widely credited with turning Mercedes into Europe's most profitable motor company, and he fiercely resisted plans by Daimler last year to merge with Mercedes. He lost the battle, and his resignation on Thursday followed news of a boardroom shakeup by Schrempp which would give Daimler direct responsibility for Mercedes.
-- CLYDE IN RENEWED EFFORT TO RESIST GULF BID

Independent UK oil company Clyde Petroleum has renewed its efforts to fight off a 432 million sterling hostile bid from Gulf Canada Resources. In its second defence document, Clyde has released figures which, it claims, make Gulf's bid look 'wholly unacceptable'. Cylde said that its 1996 operating cash flow had increased 29 per cent to 127 million stg, and that its oil production is set to expand over the next three years from 41,117 barrels per day to 60,000 in 1999. Gulf has dismissed the figures as 'pretty incredible'.
-- FINELIST PAYS 61 MILLION STERLING FOR FERRARIS

Finelist, the vehicle parts distributor which floated in 1994, has announced that it is to buy Ferraris Piston Service from Tomkins for a total of 61 million stg. The deal is fast- growing Finelist's biggest acquisition since its float, and follows the 46.3 million stg purchase of Motor World Group last year. The Ferraris deal will make Finelist one of the UK's largest retailers of replacement clutches, brakes and engine parts. For a full range of news monitoring services.
